title: Halo: Dreamcast Evolved is "Unpolished", you guys. A random YouTube comment told me, and we always know those are the TR
title_en:
Halo: Dreamcast Evolved is "Unpolished", you guys. A random YouTube comment told me, and we always know those are the TRUE experts.

*literally runs better than 95% of the Dreamcast library and is technically far more complex than all of them*

I love when someone compliments me whilst slapping me across the face. Yeah, you do better then. I'll wait. 😂🤣

It's like IGN and everyone else who covers this game is so obsessed with the game dropping below 30 fps that I think they completely forgot how the majority of every retail game on Dreamcast runs like crap outside of fighting games, let alone the original itself on Xbox also suffering from sub 30 drops when it got heavy. Halo literally runs better than most retail Dreamcast games and it looks better than all of them.

People have NO IDEA how much effort it took to get this game to both look and run this well on Dreamcast. There is no "Durr, Claude, put Halo and Dreamcast and make it run real good!"

I've been doing gamedev as a hobby for 26 years and oversaw every implementation from code quality to MCP servers, spent hundreds of dollars out-of-pocket, and numerous 3-4 hours night sleep to get this game to its current state so people can play the game FOR FREE on their Dreamcast while simultaneously inventing new graphical techniques for the DC like soft self shadowing.

If you think this is some slop code port, then feel free to ask @falco_girgis who has seen it himself.

But hey, it's unpolished, right?

title_en:
The EVM is a courtroom, not a calculator. It rules on agreements, but it grinds numbers slowly.

Every judgment call on @GenLayer still lands on a chain that charges gas to record the result.

When an autonomous agent needs to evaluate an ambiguous outcome, the math behind that thought is expensive on a standard virtual machine.

The GenLayer Chain now runs on the @arbitrum stack. That stack ships Stylus beside the EVM.

Stylus runs contracts written in Rust. They compile to WebAssembly before execution.

The rules stay in Solidity.
The heavy math can move to Rust.
The chain hosts both engines.

Training the model is not the hard part of onchain AI. Paying the gas bill for every thought in production is.

A cheaper lane for heavy code is what turns autonomous workflows from experiments into products.

Same courtroom, new calculator.

What is the one bottleneck in your codebase or daily workflow that cheaper compute would clear first?

title_en:
₦2,750 left my account. Iya Fatima said she hadn’t received a kobo.

At NYSC camp in Cross River, I’d ordered rice, beans, plantain and two pieces of meat.

I transferred the money. My banking app showed “successful.” I showed her the receipt.

She still couldn’t confirm the payment.

Same counter. Same payment. Two different accounts of what happened.

That moment came back to me when I read about @GenLayer moving its public chain to @arbitrum.

That dispute taught me something: a transaction record doesn’t always settle whether an obligation was fulfilled.

Now imagine an AI agent submitting work on your behalf. The submission can be recorded onchain. Whether it meets the agreed terms may still need judgment.

That’s the problem GenLayer is building an adjudication layer to address.

Validators using different AI models evaluate judgment-dependent questions through Optimistic Democracy. Intelligent Contracts execute in GenVM on validator nodes.

The GenLayer Chain coordinates the process: transaction ordering, committee assignments, votes, appeals, staking and final outcomes.

That chain moved. The adjudication protocol didn’t.

GenLayer migrated its public chain from Matter Labs’ ZK Stack to Arbitrum Nitro, with Conduit operating the infrastructure. Optimistic Democracy, GenVM and validator responsibilities remain unchanged.

Nitro’s Geth-based architecture supports familiar Ethereum tools. Arbitrum also brings GenLayer closer to builders developing judgment-dependent applications.

Bradbury is already running on Nitro. GenLayer’s work with Matter Labs continues through Prividium for private, permissioned institutional deployments.

I still remember the word “successful” on my screen while Iya Fatima waited for confirmation on hers.

If an AI agent marked a job “successful,” what kind of task would make you question that verdict before accepting it?

title_en:
Today I interviewed another ML Engineer candidate with 6 years of experience. 

Same pattern, same behavior, rejected. What’s common in these rejections?

Weak foundations, reliance on vibe-coded projects, and inability to explain the why and how of their work.

He described a project using dictionary lookup and OCR. When I asked why a dictionary over a vector DB, or why not an LLM for PDFs containing images rather than text, he threw out terms like Lambda, ECS, Bedrock, and harnesses without even surface-level knowledge.

On the deep learning assessment, he had vibe-coded the project but didn’t know sigmoid, softmax, or vanishing gradients. He also had no idea about TF-IDF or BERT, despite listing related projects.

His resume looked strong with real-time experience and he was hired around 2021–2022 and hasn’t interviewed since. Complete reliance on vibe coding has eroded his basics.

Same pattern observed:

1. Almost no one focuses on ML basics now and they are essential.

2. When discussing vibe-coded projects, cover HLD, fallbacks, latency optimizations, and why you chose X over Y.

3. Don’t start with buzzwords. Start with the business problem, what you built, what you did when it broke, and the impact.

Most importantly, keep building something every day. The gap is hard to close.

I have two more interviews coming up and will share those too.

title_en:
An AI agent saying “I can help with research” doesn’t tell me enough to hire it.

Research what, exactly?

Can it compare protocols, collect onchain data, identify risks, or produce a report with verifiable sources?

There’s a big difference between listing a capability and presenting a service someone can confidently pay for.

That’s one part of the agent economy I’m interested in exploring through @termix_ai and https://t.co/VQiubSQwfg

A useful agent service listing should make a few things clear:

• The problem it solves: what can someone actually hire this agent to do?

• The deliverable: what will the client receive at the end?

• The scope: what is included, and what isn’t?

• The expectations: what does a successful result look like?

This matters because discovery is only the beginning.

An agent might have impressive capabilities, but if a potential client cannot understand the service or what they will receive, turning that discovery into a real job becomes difficult.

With https://t.co/VQiubSQwfg, agents can create service listings that people can discover and purchase.

I like looking at this from the client’s side too. Before hiring an agent, I want to know what I’m buying, not just how intelligent its description sounds.

The agent economy will need capable agents, yes. But it will also need agents that know how to present their work as a clear, useful service.

That’s how skills start becoming commerce.

title_en:
If I was 22 and broke, I'd do this TONIGHT:

> learn GTM engineering in 30 days
> pick one type of B2B company
> map every company in their market
> book them sales calls with AI
> charge $3K a month per company
> hit $10K months inside 6 months
> quit your job
> move into your own place
> book the trip you keep putting off

Here's EXACTLY how to do the first six:

0. WHAT THE JOB IS (30 SECONDS)

Every B2B company needs a steady flow of new customers.

Plenty of them still rely on referrals and whoever the founder knows.

A GTM engineer builds the system that finds every company that could buy and books sales calls with them.

The title barely existed before 2024, and job postings for it grew 205% in a year.

Vercel and OpenAI pay $250K+ for it, and the median salary sits at $127.5K.

You can sell the same work straight to companies and skip the job application.

1. LEARN THE STACK (30 DAYS)

Spend week one on who buys and why, before you open a single tool.

Then learn 4 tools and ignore everything else for now.

Clay is where the lists get built, and Claude Code handles the research and first drafts.

Add n8n to move replies into Slack and the CRM, and EmailBison to send.

2. PICK ONE TYPE OF COMPANY (ONE WEEKEND)

Their customers need to be worth $10K+ each.

The market has to hold 50,000+ companies, and under 10,000 you're better off going account by account.

And somebody on their side has to take the calls you book.

Boring industries are the easiest to start in.

A building contractor's inbox has a supplier invoice in it and not much else, so your email gets read.

3. MAP THEIR WHOLE MARKET (ONE WEEK, $0 TO START)

Pull companies from Apollo's free plan and Google Maps, then stack industry directories on top.

Have AI read every company's website and score it against the client's best customers.

Tell it what a bad fit looks like too, and cut anything under 80%.

Find the emails with a waterfall: Icypeas → Prospeo → LeadMagic, with BlitzAPI for phone numbers

Then verify everything with MillionVerifier and run the catch-alls through BounceBan.

We mapped 69,204 businesses off Google Maps for one client, and it booked them 53 meetings in 50 days.

4. SET UP SENDING (14 DAYS)

Buy secondary domains on Porkbun, and never send from the client's real one.

Get inboxes from ScaledMail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC on every domain.

Warm them for 14 days before a single cold email goes out.

Cap each inbox at 15 cold emails a day and turn open tracking off.

When you need more volume, add inboxes instead of pushing the ones you have.

5. WRITE THE EMAIL (ONE AFTERNOON)

Keep it under 65 words, and under 40 if it's going to an Outlook inbox.

Open with one real detail about their business.

Our AI-written first lines hit a 0.27% reply rate.

A campaign that used the prospect's own project and location hit 14.5%.

Close on something free they can say yes to, like a sample list or a mockup of their own work.

Give every version 1,000+ sends before you decide it doesn't work.

6. CATCH EVERY REPLY (SAME DAY)

Build an n8n flow that tags each reply by intent and posts the good ones into Slack.

Answer inside a minute, then pick up the phone and call them.

Contacting a lead within a minute lifts conversions by 391% (Velocify).

Offer 2 times inside the next 2 days ("Tuesday at 11 or Wednesday at 2?") instead of sending a calendar link.

Judge every campaign on contacts per lead: under 500 is good, around 1,000 needs a tweak, and 2,000+ means the offer's wrong.

Run the numbers at $3K a month:

1 client = $3K
4 clients = $12K
10 clients = $30K

GTM engineering is where data science was in 2012.

The people who'll regret missing it are sitting in SDR seats right now.

Nobody has ever needed a tutorial on quitting their job.

Our Head of GTM wrote a 40-page guide on every part of GTM engineering.

Comment "GTM" and I'll send it over (must be following)

Get inboxes from ScaledMail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC on every domain.

title_en:
was reading @Acurast's new post about the Microsoft outage on November 12, and one part got me thinking.

Outlook, Teams and Copilot were all affected by the same outage. Different services, but they still depended on the same company's infrastructure.

Acurast points out something interesting here.

Instead of running everything in one cloud, developers can spread their workloads across phones in different countries. If one phone goes offline, other phones running the same workload can keep working.

Their network now has over 360,000 phones across 175+ countries, according to the latest blog.

But I think there's an important difference.

Acurast can't magically fix Outlook when Microsoft's servers go down. And an AI agent that needs Outlook's API would still have problems.

What it can do is help keep independent tasks running, like monitoring services or sending alerts through another system.

I'd actually like to see Acurast test this in public. Take one Processor offline while a real application is running and show how the network handles it.

That would tell us more about reliability than just counting connected phones.

full_text_zh:
11 月 12 日，我正在阅读 @Acurast 关于 Microsoft 宕机事件的新帖子，其中一个内容引起了我的思考。

Outlook、Teams 和 Copilot 均受到同一故障的影响。不同的服务，但它们仍然依赖于同一家公司的基础设施。

阿库拉斯特在这里指出了一些有趣的事情。

开发人员可以将工作负载分散到不同国家/地区的手机上，而不是在一个云中运行所有内容。如果一部电话离线，运行相同工作负载的其他电话可以继续工作。

根据最新博客，他们的网络目前在 175 多个国家/地区拥有超过 360,000 部电话。

但我认为有一个重要的区别。

当 Microsoft 的服务器出现故障时，Acurast 无法神奇地修复 Outlook。而需要 Outlook API 的 AI 代理仍然会遇到问题。

它可以做的是帮助保持独立任务的运行，例如监控服务或通过另一个系统发送警报。

我实际上希望看到 Acurast 公开测试这一点。在实际应用程序运行时使一个处理器离线并显示网络如何处理它。

这将告诉我们更多关于可靠性的信息，而不仅仅是计算连接的电话。

title_en:
“Delivered” can start an argument as easily as end one.

Imagine an agent ordering steel for a project. The shipment arrives. The buyer disputes whether it meets the specification.

Both agents have a reason to say they’re right. Who settles it?

That’s the lens I’m using for @GenLayer move to the @arbitrum stack.

The GenLayer Chain moved from ZK Stack to Nitro. It hosts the consensus contracts that track who judges a case, their votes, appeals and the final outcome.

The method of judgment stays the same. Validators running different AI models reach agreement through Optimistic Democracy. Intelligent contracts still execute in GenVM on validator nodes.

My take: the rules for resolving a disagreement should survive a change in the infrastructure recording it. GenLayer preserved that boundary while moving its chain to a stack with years of production use.

For anyone building agents that spend money, here’s a question worth answering before the first purchase:

What would your agent need to see before accepting “job done”?

title_en:
A court does not run its own power grid. GenLayer, the adjudication layer for AI agents, follows a similar split.

Its chain moved to Arbitrum Nitro, the same software behind the chain Robinhood launched in July.

That chain is operated with Conduit, a company whose whole business is running chains, with more than 60 mainnets on its platform. The GenLayer team keeps its hands on the protocol.

I like that division of labour. Optimistic Democracy, GenVM and intelligent contracts are where GenLayer's judgment lives, and the move leaves them as they were. Validators keep the same role, and their nodes now connect to the new chain.

The next phase of the Bradbury testnet went live the same day. The work with ZKsync continues on Prividium and enterprise, while the public network is the part that moved.

@GenLayer chose a stack that others already run on, and @arbitrum is where many of the builders it wants to work with already are.

Would you rather a protocol team run its own chain, or leave that part to specialists?

What actually happens inside an AI agent?

An AI agent is more than an LLM connected to a prompt. It follows a continuous workflow where it receives information, reasons, accesses memory, plans tasks, and executes actions.

Here's a breakdown of the architecture behind modern AI agents.

𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘’𝗦 𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗜𝗧 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞𝗦:

01 — 𝗜𝗡𝗣𝗨𝗧 & 𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗖𝗘𝗣𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

The starting point where an agent receives and understands incoming information.

→ User text and instructions

→ API calls

→ Sensor data

→ Events and triggers

02 — 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗦𝗢𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗘𝗡𝗚𝗜𝗡𝗘 / 𝗟𝗟𝗠

The brain of the agent that analyzes information and decides what to do next.

→ Chain-of-Thought

→ ReAct

→ Plan-and-Execute

→ Decision-making

03 — 𝗠𝗘𝗠𝗢𝗥𝗬 𝗦𝗬𝗦𝗧𝗘𝗠

Allows agents to retain information and maintain context across tasks.

→ Short-term: Conversation context and working state.

→ Long-term: Vector stores and episodic memory.

→ Learned patterns: Previously stored information.

04 — 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗟𝗘

Breaks complex goals into smaller tasks and organizes their execution.

→ Goal decomposition

→ Task sequencing

→ Step-by-step execution

→ Progress tracking

Example:

→ Step 1: Understand the goal.

→ Step 2: Break it into subtasks.

→ Step 3: Execute each step.

05 — 𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗟 𝗘𝗫𝗘𝗖𝗨𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 / 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

This is where agents interact with external systems and perform real actions.

→ Model Context Protocol (MCP)

→ API calls

→ Code execution

→ Database queries

→ File system

→ External services like GitHub

Results are sent back to the reasoning engine for further processing.

06 — 𝗚𝗨𝗔𝗥𝗗𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗟𝗦 & 𝗦𝗔𝗙𝗘𝗧𝗬

Keeps agent operations within defined security boundaries.

→ Permission controls

→ Approval gates

→ Content filtering

→ Rate limits

→ Human-in-the-loop checkpoints

07 — 𝗢𝗕𝗦𝗘𝗥𝗩𝗔𝗕𝗜𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

Monitors agent activities and helps developers maintain system reliability.

→ Execution tracing

→ Error monitoring

→ Workflow tracking

→ Performance monitoring

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞𝗙𝗟𝗢𝗪:

Input
↓
Perception
↓
Reasoning + Memory
↓
Can the agent answer directly?

→ YES: Generate output.

→ NO: Move to planning and tool execution.

Planning
↓
Tool Execution
↓
Results
↓
Goal Evaluation
↓
Final Output

If the goal isn't achieved, the agent returns to reasoning and planning to continue the task.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗞𝗘𝗬 𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡:

An AI agent isn't just a language model. It's a complete system where reasoning, memory, planning, tools, safety, and monitoring work together.

Understanding this architecture is the first step toward building AI agents that can actually complete real-world tasks.

An AI agent is more than an LLM connected to a prompt. It follows a continuous workflow where it receives information, reasons, accesses memory, plans tasks, and executes actions.

Here's a breakdown of the architecture behind modern AI agents.

→ User text and instructions

→ API calls

→ Sensor data

→ Events and triggers

The brain of the agent that analyzes information and decides what to do next.

→ Chain-of-Thought

→ ReAct

→ Plan-and-Execute

→ Decision-making

03 — 𝗠𝗘𝗠𝗢𝗥𝗬 𝗦𝗬𝗦𝗧𝗘𝗠

Allows agents to retain information and maintain context across tasks.

→ Short-term: Conversation context and working state.

→ Long-term: Vector stores and episodic memory.

→ Learned patterns: Previously stored information.

04 — 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗟𝗘

→ Goal decomposition

→ Task sequencing

→ Step-by-step execution

→ Progress tracking

→ Step 1: Understand the goal.

→ Step 2: Break it into subtasks.

→ Step 3: Execute each step.

→ Code execution

→ File system

→ Error monitoring

→ Workflow tracking

→ Performance monitoring

Why would GenLayer run on two paths at once?

So the move does not shrink the plan. It gives each customer the right door. And Bradbury going live on the new stack the same day shows it is already running.

Which door do you think brings in more builders first, public or private?

full_text_zh:
为什么 GenLayer 会同时在两条路径上运行？

想象一下同一天走进来的两个顾客。

第一个是一个构建人工智能代理应用程序的小团队。他们想要一个公共网络、开放工具和已经在附近的构建器。对于他们来说，GenLayer 的公共网络现在在 @arbitrum 堆栈上运行。 Nitro 是围绕 Geth 构建的，因此普通的以太坊工具可以按原样工作。 Robinhood 在同一软件上运行自己的链。

第二个是银行集团。他们想要在彼此之间结算合同，而这不能放在公共链上。对于他们来说，@GenLayer 继续与 Matter Labs 合作开发 Prividium（一个私有的、经过许可的版本）。

两种不同的需求，相同的引擎。乐观民主、GenVM 和智能合约的工作原理是一样的。改变的只是合约接触链的地方：桥、以太坊链接和天然气处理。

因此此举并没有缩小计划。它为每个客户提供了正确的大门。 Bradbury 于同一天在新堆栈上上线，表明它已经在运行。

title_en:
Final grade. Wrong number. Zero alerts.

I found it when I checked my result against my own records. The score was lower than I had calculated. I went through each mark, found the gap and asked my lecturer for the full breakdown. One record had been omitted. It was corrected.

What it left me with: a result means nothing if the process behind it stays hidden.

That stays with me every time I look at @GenLayer moving its coordination chain to @arbitrum.

GenLayer adjudicates for the agentic economy. AI validators running distinct models dispute judgment calls and converge through Optimistic Democracy. Intelligent Contracts execute in GenVM. Moving to Arbitrum Nitro positions that layer where many of the builders who will need it are already operating.

What relocated to Nitro, operated by Conduit:

- Sequencing, committee formation, vote tallies, appeals and staked resolutions
- Bridge mechanics, Ethereum interface handling and gas accounting

What stayed fully intact:

Yeah, absol
title_en:
I love the idea of an AI agent managing my DeFi portfolio.

But giving it unrestricted access to my wallet?

Yeah, absolutely not. 😂

And apparently, the people building @termix_ai have been thinking about this problem too.

I was going through the AACP whitepaper and found something called Vault Extension.

We have already talked about agents getting hired, completing jobs, and earning USDC.

But managing someone else's money is a completely different story.

Imagine I want an AI agent to manage $2000 across DeFi protocols.

Maybe move liquidity between pools, optimize yield, or rebalance positions when market conditions change.

I want the agent to make decisions.

What I do not want is for it to wake up one morning and send my entire balance to some random address. 💀

This is the problem TermiX wants to address with its StrategyVault and TransactionGuard architecture.

The idea is pretty clever.

Instead of handing an agent control over your wallet, you deposit capital into a dedicated smart contract.

You define the permissions before the job begins.

For example:
→ The agent can interact with approved protocols like Aave or Uniswap.

→ Only specific smart contract functions are permitted.

→ Arbitrary withdrawals and unauthorized transfers are blocked.

→ A stop-loss threshold and execution deadline can be configured.

The agent gets room to execute its strategy, but only within the boundaries you have established.

And the entire transaction history remains onchain.

I particularly like the distinction here.

The agent does not need unrestricted control over your money to do useful work with it.

Of course, smart contract vulnerabilities, bad oracle data, and market crashes are still real risks. Even a well-designed permission system cannot eliminate them.

And Vault Extension is a proposed component of AACP, not something I am treating as a finished production feature.

Still, I think this gives us a glimpse of where TermiX could eventually go.

Today we are discussing AI agents earning $50 for research reports.

Tomorrow, we might be discussing agents managing DAO treasuries, allocating liquidity, and executing financial strategies under programmable restrictions.

That is a much more interesting direction for the agent economy.

I do not need an AI agent that promises to be responsible with my money.

I want infrastructure that limits what it can do when something goes wrong.

That is the part I would like to see TermiX deliver.

显然，构建 @termix_ai 的人们也一直在思考这个问题。

我正在浏览 AACP 白皮书，发现了一个叫做 Vault Extension 的东西。

我们已经讨论过代理被雇用、完成工作和赚取 USDC。

但管理别人的钱是一个完全不同的故事。

想象一下，我想要一个 AI 代理来跨 DeFi 协议管理 2000 美元。

也许可以在资金池之间转移流动性，优化收益率，或者在市场条件发生变化时重新平衡头寸。

我希望代理人做出决定。

我不希望它在一天早上醒来并将我的全部余额发送到某个随机地址。 💀

这就是 TermiX 希望通过其 StrategyVault 和 TransactionGuard 架构解决的问题。

这个想法相当聪明。

您无需将钱包的控制权交给代理，而是将资金存入专用的智能合约。

您可以在作业开始之前定义权限。

例如：
→ 代理可以与 Aave 或 Uniswap 等经批准的协议进行交互。

→ 仅允许特定的智能合约功能。

→ 阻止任意提款和未经授权的转账。

→ 可以配置止损阈值和执行期限。

代理有空间执行其策略，但仅限于您建立的边界内。

整个交易历史记录都保留在链上。

我特别喜欢这里的区别。

代理人不需要对您的资金进行无限制的控制就可以用它来做有用的工作。

当然，智能合约漏洞、不良预言机数据和市场崩溃仍然是真正的风险。即使设计良好的许可系统也无法消除它们。

Vault Extension 是 AACP 提议的组件，而不是我将其视为已完成的生产功能的东西。

尽管如此，我认为这让我们了解了 TermiX 最终的发展方向。

今天我们讨论的是通过研究报告赚取 50 美元的人工智能代理。

明天，我们可能会讨论代理管理 DAO 金库、分配流动性以及在可编程限制下执行财务策略。

对于代理经济来说，这是一个更有趣的方向。

我不需要一个承诺对我的钱负责的人工智能代理。

我希望基础设施能够在出现问题时限制其所能执行的操作。

这就是我希望看到 TermiX 交付的部分。

代理人不需要对您的资金进行无限制的控制就可以用它来做有用的工作。

尽管如此，我认为这让我们了解了 TermiX 最终的发展方向。

今天我们讨论的是通过研究报告赚取 50 美元的人工智能代理。

明天，我们可能会讨论代理管理 DAO 金库、分配流动性以及在可编程限制下执行财务策略。

I added a confidence gate between Grok and Fable 5.2.

Ou
title_en:
CUT MY REVERSE ENGINEERING COSTS BY 67% WITH ONE SIMPLE GATE.

I added a confidence gate between Grok and Fable 5.2.

Out of 400 tasks, 363 went straight to the cheaper model.

Here's how it works:

→ REA decompiles each function into pseudocode.
→ Grok analyzes it and returns a job, confidence score, and reason for uncertainty.
→ Everything is returned as structured JSON.

The 0.8 threshold decides what happens next.

Above 0.8 → Grok handles it.
Below 0.8 → Fable 5.2 takes over.

The results:

• Grok only: 41 min, $1.80, 19 unknowns.
• Fable only: 26 min, $9.40, 4 unknowns.
• Hybrid: 33 min, $3.10, 5 unknowns.

That's a 67% cost reduction compared with using Fable for everything.

Fable maps inputs, outputs, and side effects while classifying every claim as observation, inference, or unknown.

The smartest part?

Don't send every task to your most expensive model. Let confidence decide when extra intelligence is worth the cost.

Start at 0.8. Adjust the threshold based on which model gets the final call right.

Less waste. Lower costs. Smarter AI workflows.

title: We're getting to the point where AI isn't just answering research questions, it's actually helping carry out the researc
title_en:
We're getting to the point where AI isn't just answering research questions, it's actually helping carry out the research itself.

@DeepPrinciple's Mira Science lets researchers coordinate teams of AI scientists, connect them to professional tools and cloud compute, and run entire research workflows.

that's a pretty big leap from typing a question into ChatGPT and hoping for a good response.

the idea of multiple AI agents working through scientific problems together is pretty crazy when you think about it.

could genuinely change how research gets done over the next few years.
title_zh:
我们已经达到这样的程度：人工智能不仅可以回答研究问题，而且实际上可以帮助开展研究本身。

@DeepPrinciple 的 Mira Science 让研究人员能够协调人工智能科学家团队，将他们连接到专业工具和云计算，并运行整个研究工作流程
